note: The 1st, 4th and 5th chords found as neighbours on the circle of fifths (chords-of-a-key:1): counted the long way once as chord tokens, their roots ringed on the staff, followed over a backing track in C, then read off the circle and called out in a new order in G, the second key. The circle is the lesson, so C and G are fixed and there are no moves.

exercise.title: The 1st, 4th and 5th chords, found on the circle
exercise.why: The three major chords of a key are built on its 1st, 4th and 5th notes, and on the circle of fifths they sit side by side, so the circle finds them in any key.

cells.text:
{{chord:I}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}. {{chord:IV}} is the 4th chord, built on {{4}}. {{chord:V}} is the 5th chord, built on {{5}}.
The circle of fifths below is on C major, and the keys marked beside it on the outer ring are those three chords. Tap {{chord:IV}} to hear it: the circle moves there, so tap {{chord:I}} to come back. Do the same with {{chord:V}}.
On the staff below, tap the three ringed notes, {{1}}, {{4}} and {{5}}: each one is the root of one of those chords.

Press Play below to start the backing track: {{chord:I}}, {{chord:IV}}, {{chord:V}} and back to {{chord:I}}, one bar each. Say the number of each chord as it arrives, 1, 4 or 5, with the lit chord box to help.
Practice until you hear a change coming before the box lights.
The circle below is on G major. Read its 1st, 4th and 5th chords off the marked keys on the outer ring before you listen.

Press Play below to start the backing track in G: the same three chords in a new order. Look away and say the number of each chord, then look back at the lit chord box to check.
In G the chords have other names, and each number keeps its sound: the 1st chord still sounds like home.
